summary: North-end breakwater light at Buffalo Harbor, Lake Erie: lit 1872, rebuilt 1912-14, struck by a freighter in 1958, replaced by a 71-foot tower in 1961.

notes_for_editor: 1) Position. The Board's name is 'Buffalo Breakwater, north end' (cite 6). LighthouseFriends puts the 1872 light at the southern end of the outermost breakwater (cite 3). The 1961 tower is at the end of the farthest breakwater (cite 5), the south end of the outer (detached) breakwater (cite 18), and the southern end of the outermost breakwater (cite 3); all three agree. Rowlett's Middle Reef entry (cite 18) belongs to the Horseshoe Reef light, not to this station, and is not used. The USLHS position (42 52'39", 78 53'56"; cite 1) is about 0.8 km from the record point, which matches LighthouseFriends' coordinates. The record point was kept. 2) Tower material and height. USLHS gives iron and 53.5 ft above water (cite 1); LighthouseFriends gives timber and a 37 ft focal plane (cite 3), and the Buffalo site gives 37 ft above the lake (cite 4). The story states the disagreement. 3) Colour of the 1872 light. The Buffalo site says fixed red (cite 4); LighthouseFriends does not give a colour. 4) Radio beacon year: 1925 (cite 5) or 15 April 1927 (cite 3). The Bulletin of 1925 only says the service contemplated radio fog signals there (cite 16); the 1924-1929 index lists a radio beacon (cite 17). 5) 1958 collision. Cites 3 and 5 agree on the freighter, date and damage; they name different keepers. The collisions of 1899, 1900, 1909 and 1910 come from two secondary sources only (cites 3, 4). 6) Keepers. Every roster line comes from the USLHS archive (cites 1, 2), which takes it from NARA keeper registers via the Kraig Anderson inventory. None of these lines has been confirmed in a primary record. The 1958 keeper name (George Harrington) comes from LighthouseFriends only. Lines marked 'at least' carry no end year; Coast Guard lines from 1952 may run past 1960 and are named only as the archive prints them. 7) Names matched by position: none in the story. The Board's keeper tables were not read. 8) Fiscal years, checked against the scanned volumes' year headers: the 'ineffi-cient' recommendation (cite 6, scan 189) is in the report for the year ended 30 June 1891, not 1892; the 1892 report (scan 524) renews it as 'ineffective'. The keeper-dwelling move (scan 190, cite 19) is in the report for the year ended 30 June 1893; the 352-hour figure (scan 511, cite 7) is in the report for the year ended 30 June 1894. 9) Not found: the Board's annual reports for 1872-1890 are not in the local corpus, so the 1870-1872 construction and the 1899-1910 collisions rest on secondary sources. No newspaper for the 1958 collision was found. The USCG Historian's archived page for this light was not reachable (the archive copies tried returned 404). 10) Not used or removed: the Life-Saving Service reports for 1880-1881 (schooners against 'the old breakwater', not named as this light); the Light Vessel No. 82 loss of 1913 (a separate station, removed from the story and from the events). 11) The 'first diaphone in the United States' claim (cite 3) is not verified. 12) The 1962 relief of the port's last Coast Guard keepers (cite 5) is not tied to a named light in the source.
